transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood CSM), Liam O'Connor (Verdigris Head of ML), Sara Patel (Verdigris Platform), Noah Rivera (Verdigris CTO)

Summary: quick discovery to size latency/throughput needs for Verdigris real-time fraud scoring + customer messages. Focus on p95 targets, concurrent streaming sessions, and whether dedicated capacity or hosted API makes sense.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): all right everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood inference, ethan's our se, priya will be on the customer success side. how's everyone doing?
00:06 Speaker 2 (Noah): good, thanks. excited to dig in. we've got about 45 minutes.
00:12 Speaker 1 (Maya): perfect, quick agenda: we want to understand your workloads — p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behaviour, security constraints — and make sure we can propose either hosted, dedicated, or private options that match. liam, do you want to kick off with what you're trying to build?
00:24 Speaker 3 (Liam): yeah thanks. so at a high level, verdigris uses an ensemble — smaller transformer reranker + a larger LLM for contextual enrichments — for fraud scoring on transactions and for customer support auto-replies. the fraud scoring path is the tighter latency target — we need the model to return within our p95 window before the transaction authorisation timeout. currently that's about p95 <= 350ms for a ~128 token response, ideally closer to 250ms.
00:50 Speaker 4 (Sara): also we have spikes, right — batch settlement windows and marketing pushes create concurrency bursts. typical baseline concurrency is 40-60 qps, bursts up to 250 concurrent requests for short windows. streaming is used for customer support flows (progressive responses), not for fraud path, but we want streaming latency to feel realtime — p95 sub 500ms for the first token and steady token/sec after.
01:18 Speaker 2 (Ethan): okay so two distinct patterns: low-latency single-turn reranker path (tight p95) and streaming multi-token chat path. both have different sweet spots for batching and caching. for the reranker the key is minimizing queueing and tail latencies — dedicated capacity with pinned GPUs often helps, but there are also routing and autoscaling policies we can apply on hosted.
01:36 Speaker 3 (Liam): question — do you have real numbers for p95 on your hosted API for, say, 7B and 13B models at 128 tokens? we need to compare with our in-house numbers.
01:45 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes, rough ballpark: hosted for a well-optimized 13B quantized model — p95 single-request (non-streaming) at 128 tokens is around 180–260 ms under moderate load (10-50 concurrent). but the tail grows with concurrency unless you have dedicated or reserved pools. for 7B it's lower — 120–180 ms. these are approximate and depend on prompt complexity, tokenization, and whether KV cache hits apply.
02:10 Speaker 4 (Sara): okay that matches roughly. our internal baseline on our self-hosted cluster is around 220–300ms for a 13B but our tail gets worse during spikes. what's the throughput in tokens/sec you see for these models when streaming?
02:24 Speaker 2 (Ethan): streaming throughput — once streaming has warmed up, token generation rates are model-dependent: a quantized 13B on good infra is ~100–250 tokens/sec per sequence depending on batch size and parallelism; 7B is often 200–400 tokens/sec. again that applies once the model is producing tokens; the first-token latency is usually higher. for sustained high-concurrency you can scale horizontally or use batching but batching increases tail.
02:50 Speaker 3 (Liam): so for fraud scoring we cannot afford batching delays. we'd rather accept a higher per-token cost for consistent tail. is that where dedicated comes in?
02:58 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes dedicated gives you reserved plans and pinned capacity, so you avoid noisy neighbour effects. we also have smart routing with fallbacks to smaller variants if capacity is constrained — that keeps the API up. but if your requirement is strict p95 < 300ms at 200 concurrent steady requests, dedicated is the safer route.
03:18 Speaker 1 (Maya): curious — what's your expected monthly token volume for this fraud path vs support chat?
03:24 Speaker 3 (Liam): fraud path is relatively small in tokens but high QPS during peak hours — estimate 50–200k requests/day, average response 100 tokens; support chat is larger token volume but lower concurrency, maybe 5–10M tokens/month.
03:40 Speaker 4 (Sara): and security-wise we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), audit logs and KMS for keys. for private deployments we might need VPC peering or on-prem.
03:52 Speaker 1 (Maya): we cover SOC2, SSO, and provide audit logs; our Private offering supports VPC and on-prem installs with customer-managed KMS. we'll share the security pack after the call.
04:03 Speaker 5 (Noah): for the pilot we want to see real numbers under our traffic: p95, 99th, error rate, and cost per 1M tokens. can you do a benchmark that simulates bursts to 250 concurrent and steady 50 qps?
04:16 Speaker 2 (Ethan): absolutely. recommended plan is a mixed-workload benchmark: 60% small 128-token reranker requests, 40% streaming 400-token chat-ish prompts, with bursts that emulate your traffic. we'll provide scripts that can run in your environment hitting hosted endpoints or using a dedicated trial pool.
04:34 Speaker 3 (Liam): how do you measure p95 for streaming? is it first-token or end-to-end? we care about both — first-token for user-perceived latency, and end-to-end for scoring latency.
04:44 Speaker 2 (Ethan): good call. we'll measure both: TTF (time to first token) p95 and TTE (time to end) p95. for fraud scoring we target TTE p95; for customer replies TTF p95 matters more.
04:56 Speaker 4 (Sara): network-wise, our VPC is in us-east-1. do you have regional endpoints? we'd prefer hosted in us-east during pilot to avoid cross-region latency.
05:06 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes we have regional hosting; we'll route you to us-east for the pilot. for dedicated we can colocate in your preferred region too.
05:13 Speaker 5 (Noah): can you quantify tail behavior under GC/compaction or when models reload? we observed occasional 2–3s spikes when keys recompute.
05:23 Speaker 2 (Ethan): model cold starts and KV cache misses can cause spikes. we mitigate with warm pools, sticky routing, and pre-warming for canaries. for dedicated pools you control lifecycle so these events are less disruptive. we'll instrument the benchmark to flag these events and show the percent of requests above threshold.
05:40 Speaker 3 (Liam): what about quantization tradeoffs — if we run an int8/4-bit quantized model, how much do we save and how much does latency change?
05:48 Speaker 2 (Ethan): quantization usually reduces memory and can slightly speed up throughput, but inference kernels and hardware matter; int8 often gives 20–40% lower memory use and modest latency improvements; 4-bit can save more but may affect output quality slightly. we recommend running evals on your prompts to validate quality. our Optimize product will recommend quantization profiles per workload.
06:10 Speaker 4 (Sara): for the fraud path we need deterministic-ish outputs for audits — how do you handle model versioning and rollbacks?
06:18 Speaker 1 (Maya): we support pinning model versions, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback. everything is logged and auditable; we'll provide the rollout audit example in the security pack.
06:27 Speaker 5 (Noah): let's talk success criteria: for the pilot we want p95 end-to-end for fraud <= 300ms, TTF p95 for chat <= 500ms, error rate < 0.5%, and cost baseline.
06:38 Speaker 2 (Ethan): sounds reasonable. we'll propose a benchmark matrix that targets those SLOs and shows cost/latency tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated.
06:45 Speaker 3 (Liam): what are typical tokens/sec numbers we should expect per GPU for sustained streaming? we want that to dimension dedicated pools if needed.
06:54 Speaker 2 (Ethan): on mainstream GPUs with optimized kernels, 13B quantized models often do 100–250 tokens/sec sustained per sequence; if you multiplex many sequences you can get higher aggregate tokens/sec per GPU via batching. so for planning, if you need X tokens/sec sustained, we can work out required GPU count based on your prompt mix. we'll include worked examples in the benchmark plan.
07:16 Speaker 4 (Sara): are there any built-in client libraries for running benchmarks or do we need to roll our own?
07:22 Speaker 2 (Ethan): we have a benchmark repo and scripts — load generators, sample prompt sets, and post-processing tools to compute p50/p95/p99, TTF/TTE, and token/sec. we'll share repo links and help run the first run.
07:34 Speaker 1 (Maya): logistically, maya: we will send pricing for hosted and dedicated including a reserved pilot discount. ethan: you'll own the benchmark plan. priya: you'll handle the security docs.
07:46 Speaker 5 (Noah): good. one more question — if dedicated is chosen, how quickly can you spin up a reserved pool?
07:52 Speaker 2 (Ethan): depends on capacity and region; typical lead time is 2–4 weeks for reserved pools, faster if we have available inventory. for pilots we sometimes allocate short-term burst capacity within days.
08:02 Speaker 3 (Liam): can the pilot measure cold-start behaviors and multi-tenant interference? we want both metrics.
08:09 Speaker 2 (Ethan): yes our benchmark will record cold-start incidence and correlate to percentiles. we'll also run noise-injection tests to show multi-tenant tail effects on hosted endpoints.
08:20 Speaker 4 (Sara): network egress and data residency: we need confirmation that no PII is logged and that logs can be exported to our SIEM.
08:28 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes we have configuration to disable data retention for certain routes and we support log export and customer-managed KMS. details in security pack.
08:37 Speaker 5 (Noah): ok let's recap action items.
08:40 Speaker 1 (Maya): recap: maya sends pricing + pilot terms; ethan sends benchmark plan + scripts; priya sends security pack; liam/sara share sample prompt set, target p95s, and SRE contact. cadence: follow-up tech deep-dive next tuesday.
08:56 Speaker 3 (Liam): sounds good, thanks everyone.
08:59 Speaker 1 (Maya): thanks all, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the deep-dive.
09:04 Meeting ended

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few mis-attributed lines early on (speaker labels approximate) and occasional word swaps (e.g., KV cache noted as K-V cache or KV-cache). Some technical terms spelled out inconsistently.
